Livia Marchetti-Roe was a composer best known for her music for small choirs. She was born in 1899, the daughter of a church organist in the town of Sallow. She wrote her first published piece at the age of fifteen. Her career was interrupted for ten years while she raised four children. She returned to composing in 1938 and produced more than 200 works in the following decades. Her most famous piece, Winter Vespers, lasts only six minutes and is sung without instruments. She refused to conduct her own music, saying that she preferred to listen from the back row. A festival of her music has been held in Sallow every two years since 1990.

Lake Osmira lies at an altitude of 2,310 metres in the Calvane mountains. It covers eighteen square kilometres and reaches a maximum depth of 96 metres. The water is a striking turquoise because of fine rock dust carried in by glacial streams. The lake freezes completely from November to April, and the ice can be a metre thick. A rare fish, the Osmira char, is found nowhere else in the world. Shepherds have brought their flocks to the shores every summer for at least 500 years. Motor boats were banned in 1992 to keep the water clean. A walking path of 21 kilometres circles the lake and takes about seven hours to complete.

The glaciologist Imre Solvang devoted three decades to research on the Harren ice field.
Born in a fishing village in 1921, he originally qualified as a surveyor.
The first deep ice core from the field, 310 metres long, was drilled by him in 1953.
From the layers in that core he was able to work out the snowfall of every year for nine centuries back.
He found that the ice was losing roughly half a metre of thickness annually.
At first hardly any colleagues accepted his findings, and journals turned down his key paper twice.
Aerial surveys carried out years afterwards matched his numbers nearly perfectly.
In 1988 his name was given to a research station at the margin of the ice field.

Its timber is almost black and so dense that it sinks in water. For centuries it was used for the keels of ships because it resists rot and sea worms. The method moves through the list forwards and backwards, exchanging adjacent items that are in the wrong order.

It runs in close to linear time when the list is already almost in order.

Its running time, however, increases with the square of the length of the list in the worst case.

Along the slow rivers of the Indra basin lives the copperback heron, a wading bird. The bird's back is covered in copper feathers, its throat is white, and it reaches around 70 centimetres tall. Hand picking takes place in a period of just three weeks at the start of spring. The picked leaves are dried above cedar wood fires, giving them a slightly smoky flavour. Annual production is around 40 tonnes, of which two thirds are sold abroad. At auction, the top grade fetches over 300 dollars per kilogram. According to the growers, it ought to be brewed for precisely two minutes in water at 80 degrees.

The Dunmore rowing club owes its start in 1883 to men employed at the nearby shipyard.
Next to the former customs house, on the south bank of the River Fenn, sits the boathouse.
Some 450 people belong to the club, the youngest being eleven and the oldest eighty-six.
Fourteen national championships in the eights have been won by the club, the last one in 2016.
Silver medals were brought back from the 1996 summer games by two members who rowed in the national team.
Crews are on the water by half past five in the morning, ahead of the barges that crowd the river later.
Free coaching for students at four local schools has been available since a scheme began in 2009.
In July each year, the club's regatta brings in crews from over thirty other clubs.
candidate_text: The auditorium seats 640 people on three levels arranged in a horseshoe shape. Much of the wooden stage machinery from the 1790s still works and is used in performances. The theatre was a cinema from 1931 to 1962 and then stood empty for twenty years. A campaign led by the actor Corin Ashby saved it from being torn down in 1981. Restoration took four years and uncovered painted ceilings hidden under layers of plaster. The theatre now stages about 250 performances a year, including a pantomime every December. By tradition, a single lamp is left burning on the stage whenever the building is empty.

source_text: The Zephyr-9 programme launches weather balloons from a base on the Tarrin plateau. Each balloon is filled with helium and rises to a height of about 32 kilometres. Instruments beneath the balloon measure temperature, pressure and wind every two seconds. The data is sent by radio to the ground and shared with forecasters in fourteen countries. At the top of its flight the balloon bursts, and the instruments fall slowly under a small parachute. The programme has launched two balloons every day since it began in 2007. Only about one instrument package in five is ever found and returned. Each package carries a label that offers a reward of 100 crowns to anyone who posts it back.

Ripple sort is a sorting algorithm described in 1987 by the computer scientist Dana Okonjo-Reyes. It works by passing through the list in both directions and swapping neighbours that are out of order. After each pass the distance between compared items shrinks by a fixed ratio. Okonjo-Reyes showed that a ratio of 1.3 gives the best results on random data. The algorithm needs no extra memory, which made it useful on early small computers. On lists that are already nearly sorted, it finishes in almost linear time. In the worst case, however, its running time grows with the square of the list length. Teachers often use it in introductory courses because the code fits in about ten lines.

The Brennick lighthouse stands on a rock two kilometres off the western tip of Cape Sorrow.
It was completed in 1849 after three earlier attempts were washed away by storms.
The tower is 41 metres tall and built from interlocking granite blocks.
Its light can be seen from 38 kilometres away on a clear night.
Three keepers lived there in shifts of six weeks until the light was automated in 1982.
In the winter of 1911 the keepers were cut off for 59 days because no boat could land.

Ripple sort is a sorting algorithm described in 1987 by the computer scientist Dana Okonjo-Reyes. It works by passing through the list in both directions and swapping neighbours that are out of order. After each pass the distance between compared items shrinks by a fixed ratio. source_text: Ripple sort is a sorting algorithm described in 1987 by the computer scientist Dana Okonjo-Reyes. It works by passing through the list in both directions and swapping neighbours that are out of order. After each pass the distance between compared items shrinks by a fixed ratio. candidate_text: A narrow-gauge track of 34 kilometres, the Orrin Valley railway links Pellbridge with the Dunmoor slate quarries. The line was constructed in 1871 so that slate could be moved to the coast and shipped abroad. Trains gain 420 metres in height along the way and go through eleven tunnels. The last passenger train ran in 1958, followed four years afterwards by the last load of slate. In 1976 a team of volunteers started to repair the disused line beginning with a brief stretch close to Pellbridge. Since reopening completely in 1999, the railway has transported roughly 90,000 visitors annually. Of the first steam engines, three remain in service, and the oldest was produced in 1874. Travelling the whole length requires slightly less than two hours.
